utterances.speaker: JUDGE NINIAN STEPHEN
utterances.text: We have an initial apology, we had to delay somewhat the hearing of this case to provide for the necessary adjustments to the television link. Call the afternoon case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number 97-24-I, the Prosecutor v Milan Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NINIAN STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can every one who is using the earphones hear me in a language that they understand? The accused should put his earphones on. Can you now hear me in a language you understand? THE DEFENDANT: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. These proceedings are being recorded in accordance with the Rules of the Tribunal, and that will be available to the public, and I have so ordered in an Order that I made this morning. Can I have the initial appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, please, my name is Niemann. I appear with Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff as my co-counsel and I am assisted at the bar table by Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am Igor Pantelic and I am counsel for Mr. Kovacevic. I am acting on his behalf. For a moment I am alone. I do not have co-counsel, as with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. This is an initial appearance pursuant to Rule 62 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Mr. Niemann, are you ready to proceed with the accused's plea at this initial appearance?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. The Prosecution is ready to proceed. Before your Honour proceeds with the indictment, might I draw the court's attention to a typographical error that appears in the indictment? Your Honours, at page 5 of the indictment, paragraph 7, the last line of the paragraph there is a reference there to paragraph 5. In fact that should be a reference to paragraph 4. It is a typographical error. I draw it to the court's attention and seek leave for the indictment to be amended accordingly your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You wish to have that typographical error amended?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr Pantelic do you have any objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No your Honour, I have none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Very well. That will be noted by way of amendment of a typographical error.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you have, I take it, received a copy of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Have you read it or had it read to your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, that is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Are you satisfied he understands it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You have had adequate time to confer with your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have enough time but unfortunately my client was not in situation -- he was not in the capacity to communicate with me fully in quality, because of his health condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But generally we are ready for initial appearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Very well. Your client, I take it, understands the nature of the charge of genocide brought under Article 4 of the Statute?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my -- I know your Honour you have to ask him personally first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, would you stand, please? Would you state your full name. THE DEFENDANT: My name is Milan Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: And your date of birth? THE DEFENDANT: 10th February, 1941.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: And did you get a copy of the indictment served on you? THE DEFENDANT: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: And you either read it yourself or had it read to you in a language that you understand? THE DEFENDANT: I have read it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Pantelic has been appointed your counsel. Are you satisfied with that appointment? THE DEFENDANT: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: And, as a result of discussions with your counsel, do you understand the nature of the charge of genocide that has been brought against you? THE DEFENDANT: Yes, I do understand. I understand the nature of the charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: And are you now ready to plead to that charge? THE DEFENDANT: On the counts of this indictment I am not guilty and thank. to God and the justice of this court I think I will be found not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated for the moment. Mr. Pantelic, do you require the indictment to be read out in full, which you are entitled to do, or are you prepared to waive the reading of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I request to read this indictment in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Bos, would you read the indictment or at least those portions of it which are relevant to the present accused?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. "Indictment. The prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia pursuant to her authority under Article 18 of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, charges. Simo Drljaca and Milan Kovacevic with genocide. Background. During the early morning hours of 30 April 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, you might slow down a bit so that what is being said can be interpreted and understood in that way. MR. BOS (for the Registrar): Background: During the early morning hours of 30th April 1992 Bosnian Serb forces under the direction and control of the municipality of Prijedor Crisis Staff (or Krizni Stab) seized control of the town of Prijedor. The seizure of physical control of the town and all the municipal functions was the culmination of preparations that had begun covertly in 1991, in conjunction with Bosnian Serb efforts throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and became overt in early 1992 after the public announcement by 'Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina' of the 'Republic of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina' on 9th January 1992. In the weeks following 30th April 1992, the crisis staff implemented or authorised increasingly strict restrictions on the lives of non-Serbs in the municipality of Prijedor. All non-Serbs who held positions in the municipal government organisations who did not publicly express full support for the new order and Serbian leaders were expelled from their positions. Businesses and economic organisations quickly followed in the same manner, dismissing almost all non-Serb employees. Roadblocks were set up out throughout the municipality, particularly around predominantly non-Serb villages and in Prijedor town. These roadblocks were used to prevent non-Serbs from leaving the vicinity of their homes or villages. All non-Serbs were repeatedly exhorted and warned to turn in all weapons. During this period similar types of policies and actions were being implemented in municipalities throughout the self-proclaimed Serb Republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On about 23rd May 1992, approximately three weeks after the Bosnian Serbs forcibly took control of the governmental authority in the municipality of Prijedor, a co-ordinated attack was executed by Serbian forces, including JAN units, territorial defence (TO) units, paramilitary units, and police units, combining intensively artillery and tank shelling followed by infantry assaults on Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat areas in the municipality of Prijedor. Between April and July 1992, attacks following the same pattern were being conducted by Serbian forces across Bosnia-Herzegovina, and thousands of Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat civilians, including women, children and elderly persons were systematically rounded up and interned in detention facilities or camps. These detention facilities were staffed and operated by military and police personnel and their agents, under the control of Bosnian Serb military and civilian authorities. In addition, Bosnian Serb police and military interrogators not directly assigned to the guard staff of the camps had unfettered access to all of the detention facilities and operated in conjunction with the personnel in control of these detention facilities. In the municipality of Prijedor, the majority of Muslim and Croat residents who survived the initial attack fled their homes and were seized by Serb and Bosnian Serb forces. They were then forced to march in columns bound from one or another of the prison camps or detention facilities that the Bosnian Serb authorities had established in the municipality. The Serb and Bosnian Serb forces brought many Muslims and Croats from the columns and shot or beat them on the spot. After being herded to collection areas, most prisoners were taken to the Embarks, Keraterm or Trnopolie camps. A number of both male and female prisoners were taken to the police station in Prijedor for interrogation before being taken to a camp or released. While at the police station many of the detainees were severely maltreated both physically and psychologically. During the next several weeks, the Serb and Bosnian Serb forces continued to round up Muslims and Croats from Kozarac, Prijedor town, and other places in the municipality and interned them in camps at Omarska Keraterm and Trnopolje. The final large scale military attack conducted by the Serb and Bosnian Serb forces in the municipality occurred on about 20th July 1992 against the predominantly Muslim villages in the hilly region known as the 'Brdo' on the west side of the Sana River. Many of those who had escaped capture after the attacks on the other areas of the municipality in May 1992 had fled to the 'Brdo' area. Those who survived the attack on the 'Brdo' were also taken to Omarska Keraterm and Trnopolje camps. Omarska camp was located in part of an iron ore mining complex. Keraterm camp was set up in the disused portion of the Keraterm ceramics factory. Trnopolje camp was a complex of several buildings in the village of Trnopolje including the school, a cinema, a cultural centre, and fields that surrounded them. Within the area of the Omarska mining complex that the Bosnian Serb authorities used for the camp, the camp authorities generally confined the prisoners in three different buildings: the administration building, where the interrogations took place and most of the women were confined, the garage or hangar building, and the 'Whitehouse' a small building where particularly severe beatings were administered; and on a cement courtyard area between the buildings known as the 'Pista'. There was another small building, known as the 'Red House' where prisoners were sometimes taken but most often did not emerge alive. Many of Prijedor's Muslim and Croat intellectuals, professional and political leaders were sent to Omarska. There were approximately 40 women in the camp and all of the other prisoners in the camp were men. At Keratem camp the prisoners were held in a part of a long structure that consisted of four large storage rooms originally intended to store ceramic tiles which were manufactured at the factory. The prisoners referred to these storage areas as rooms 1, 2, 3 and 4. All of the prisoners at Keratem were men, generally of military age, that is between the ages of 16 and 60. Trnopolje camp comprised a group of buildings including a school and community cultural centre. The majority of the women, children and the elderly were interned at this camp. A number of families managed to stay together, or were allowed to stay together and were interned together at Trnopolje. A number of Bosnian Muslims and Croats who were detained at Trnopolje had fled to the camp because it was far too dangerous to stay in their own homes and villages. After the camps at Omarska and Keraterm were closed the surviving prisoners were taken to the Trnopolje and Manjaca camps".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Bos, you might pause there for a moment. Mr. Pantelic, I take it that you would think it appropriate to confine the balance of the indictment to those portions that deal with your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may ask to proceed with this indictment after the pause because it is necessary for my client to be more familiar with all these counts and all these facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You would wish the portions not relating to him to be read out as well, would you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do not insist that the portion related to Mr. Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is what I mean; omit those portions. No objection, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bos, if you would continue then. MR. BOS (for the Registrar): I will omit paragraph 1 and continue with paragraph 2. "The accused Milan Kovacevic also known as 'Mico' was born in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In 1992, he served as the President of the executive board of the municipality of Prijedor, and was a member of the municipality of Prijedor Crisis Staff. He is an anaesthetist by profession and is currently serving as the director of Prijedor Hospital. Superior authority. I will omit paragraph 3, 4 and 5. I will continue with paragraph 6. "During the period from 29th April 1992 to 31st December 1992, Milan Kovacevic was both a member of the municipality of Prijedor Crisis Staff and the President of the executive board of the municipality of Prijedor. In his role as a member of the Crisis Staff, Milan Kovacevic was part of the body that held executive power in the municipality of Prijedor at all times relevant to this indictment and the body referred to in paragraph 5 above. As the President of the executive board of the municipality of Prijedor, Milan Kovacevic occupied the second most important position on the Crisis Staff, in terms of the de jure authority. He was the individual responsible for arranging the details for visits to the camps by reporters and who provided most of the information about the camps at the briefings with visitors to the crisis staff."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr Bos, at this stage I think you will have to continue by including the references to the other indictee.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Certainly. "Count 1 (Genocide). Between April 1992 and January 1993 Simo Drljaca and Milan Kovacevic did, in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by their acts and omissions, commit genocide. "Beginning in the spring of 1992, the crisis staff of the municipality of Prijedor, including Simo Drljaca and Milan Kovacevic, planned, organised and implemented the creation of a number of detention facilities or camps, including the Omarska, Keratem and Trnopolje camps. These camps were staffed and operated by military and police personnel and their agents, under the control of the Bosnian Serb military and civilian members of the crisis staff. In addition, other Bosnian Serb police, military and civilians not directly assigned to the guard staff of the camps had unfettered access to all of the detention facilities and operated in conjunction with the personnel in control of these detention facilities. In none of the camps were the detainees afforded proper judicial process and their internment was not justified by military necessity. They were detained primarily because of their religious and ethnic identification. The conditions in the Omarska, Keratem and Trnopolje camps were abject and brutal. Bosnian Serb military police and police personnel in charge of these facilities, their staff, and other persons who visited the camps, all of whom were subject to the authority and control of the crisis staff, killed, sexually assaulted, tortured, and otherwise physically and psychologically abused detainees in the camps. At Omarska and Keraterm, the camps were deliberately operated in a matter designed to inflict on the detainees conditions intended to bring about their physical destruction with the attempt to destroy, in part, the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat people as national, ethnic or religious groups. Serious violations of international humanitarian law of a similar pattern were committed in both Omarska and Keraterm camps. Detainees were continuously subjected to or forced to witness inhumane acts, including murder, rape and sexual assaults, torture, beatings and robbery as well as other forms of mental and physical abuse. Daily food rations provided to detainees amounted to starvation rations. Medical care for the detainees was insufficient or non-existent and the general hygienic conditions prevalent at these camps were grossly inadequate. At Omarska prisoners were crowded together with little or no facilities for personal hygiene. They were fed starvation rations once a day and given only a few minutes to go to the canteen area, eat and then leave. The little water they received was often foul. Prisoners had no changes of clothing and no bedding. They received no medical care. Killings and severe beatings of prisoners were common place. The camp guards, who were both police and military personnel, and others who came to the camp and physically abused the prisoners, used all manner of weapons during these beatings, including wooden batons, metal rods and tools, lengths of thick industrial cable, rifle butts and knives. Both female and male prisoners were beaten, raped, sexually assaulted, tortured and humiliated. Hundreds of the detainees, whose identities are known and unknown, did not survive the camp. Keratem camp was located at a former ceramics factory in Prijedor. Conditions for prisoners were similar to those in Omarska camp. The detainees were so cramped in the four rooms that on many occasions they could not lie down. The detainees were not permitted to move around freely in the camp. Whether detained in their rooms around the open area outside, they were only allowed to move when specifically permitted to do so, usually only to receive their starvation rations or to go to the toilet. On a daily basis, the camp leadership, camp guards, who were both police and military personnel, and others who came to the camp to abuse the detainees, subjected the detainees the inhumane conditions, physical violence, constant humiliation, degradation, degradation and fear of death. Many detainees were executed in the camp. On one night in July, 1992, more than 150 military aged men from the 'Brdo' region were executed. Severe beatings were common place. All manner of weapons were used during these beatings, including wooden batons, metal rods, baseball bats, lengths of thick industrial cable, rifle butts and knives. The beatings, sexual assaults, tortures, and other cruel and humiliating actions were generally inflicted in full view of other detainees and were accompanied by derogatory and humiliating comments to the victims or their families and general threats to the other detainees. After they were beaten, tortured, or sexually assaulted, the detainees were carried, dragged or forced to crawl back into their rooms, without any form of care for their injuries. Hundreds of detainees, whose identities are known and unknown, did not survive the camp. Trnopolje camp was established at the site of a former school and adjacent buildings in Trnopolje village. It was the largest camp and the location to which Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat women, children and the elderly were taken. Some men of military age also managed to go directly to the Trnopolje camp. The buildings in the camp were quickly filled and the remaining detainees had to find shelter in makeshift huts of plastic and excess materials or remain out in the open fields. The hygiene facilities were grossly inadequate. Minimal rations were provided on a sporadic basis, with female detainees eventually being able to leave the camp to forage for food in the surrounding village. The camp served as the staging point for the mass deportation of all those who survived the initial attacks and camp regime and also served a much more sinister purpose: the sexual assault, rape, and torture of many of the women detained there by camp personnel, who were both police and military personnel, and by other military units from the area who came to the camp for that specific purpose. In many instances, the women and girls were taken from the camp and raped, tortured, or sexually abused at other locations. In addition many prisoners, both male and female were killed, beaten and otherwise physically and psychologically maltreated by the camp personnel and other Serbs and Bosnian Serbs who were allowed into the camp. Between 30th April 1992 and 31st December 1992 Simo Drljaca and Milan Kovacevic, in concert with others, planned, instigated, and ordered the establishment of the camps at Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje and the detention therein of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from the municipality of Prijedor under conditions calculated to bring about the physical destruction of the detainees with the intent to destroy part of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat groups as such. Further, between 30th April 1992 and 31st December 1992, Simo Drljaca and Milan Kovacevic knew or had reason to know that their subordinates who staffed the detention facilities were killing or causing serious physical or mental harm to Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats with the intent to destroy them, in part, as a national, ethnic or religious group, or had done so and failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish the perpetrators thereof. By these acts and omissions Simo Drljaca and Milan Kovacevic were complicit in the commission of genocide, punishable under Articles 4(3)(e) and 7(1) and (3) of the Statute of the Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Bos. Mr. Kovacevic, will you stand? You have heard the indictment read out. How do you plead to the count that you were complicit in the commission of genocide as charged in that indictment? THE DEFENDANT: I plead the same as I said before. I have already made a statement, and I now plead the same. Previously I answered correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am afraid that you will have to be more explicit. What I am asking you is this: do you plead guilty or not guilty? THE DEFENDANT: I plead not guilty. Again thanks God and thanks to the justice of this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. You will be remanded now to the further custody of the Tribunal in the detention unit of the Tribunal until further order. Mr. Pantelic, have you read a copy or have you rather received and read any of the material, the supporting material that accompanied the indictment that has been given to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I got the material just a few minutes before this hearing. So I am now in possession of materials and I , of course, need additional time to be competent with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Of course. And that material answers the description of the material described in Rule 66, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, your Honour it is according to Rule 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Rule 73 provides for preliminary motions. Do you anticipate making any such motions? I ask that because we need to know where we go from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I intend to file some motions according to the rules of procedure in time according to the rules, which is 60 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, very well. I have made this morning an order providing for the filing of motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann, are you ready otherwise to proceed to trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we are ready to proceed to trial. I just wish to correct perhaps what is a misunderstanding. Not all of the material falling within the description of that under 66A has at this stage been disclosed. Some of the material is awaited in terms of receiving final versions of the transcript which has been tendered as part of the supporting material. And in addition to that, your Honours, there are two witness statements which were provided where orders had been made in relation to protective measures. Those two statements have not as yet been provided as well. Your Honours, in relation to those few matters we will either overcome the difficulty with respect to protective orders, receive the transcript, alternatively if we are confronted with any difficulty in that regard we will file motions before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That sounds satisfactory. Mr Pantelic, you, too, are ready to proceed to trial, of course, after you receive the additional documents that Mr. Niemann has just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I am ready to proceed to trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I do not propose to fix any date for trial. I think it would be premature to do so. But it will be, I think, desirable, I think, to fix a date for a status conference. Mr. Niemann, have you in mind any suitable date to fix for that purpose? It occurred to me that 10th October might be an appropriate date, having regard to the time limits that are provided for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That would be a suitable date for the Prosecution, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It seems a long way off, Mr. Pantelic, but have you any comment as far as that date is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As I am concerned I am completely agreed with this proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Of course, if events occur that require more time for you, you have but to apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, but I think that we shall be under this time, during this time we can arrange that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Very well. I will fix, therefore, the 10th October as the date presently fixed for the first status conference in this matter. If, and I address now both parties, if there are any problems that arise in the meantime no doubt the Trial Chamber will be advised of them, through the Registrar, and we will see if we can meet those problems and dispose of them. Is there anything else outstanding, Mr Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not from the point of view of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: And Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Not from the point of view of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Very well. The Chamber will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: take place on 10th October, 1997)
